title: She Sold Cupcakes at 18 for Rs 20. Then She Built Dream a Dozen With Rs 5,000
excerpt: Megna Jain hid cupcakes under her Christ University desk, launched Dream a Dozen in 2018, survived a six-week COVID closure, and built a women-led Bengaluru bakery.
body:
• Megna Jain started selling eggless cupcakes at 18 as a BCom student at Christ University in Bengaluru — a WhatsApp post to her class brought an order for 90 cupcakes.
  • She launched Dream a Dozen in January 2018 from her home kitchen with an initial investment of just Rs 5,000, according to YourStory.
  • When COVID-19 hit weeks after a move to a larger space in March 2020, the bakery closed for six weeks, pivoted fully online, and recovered through corporate Diwali gift boxes — about 1,500 of them, she told YourStory.
  • Dream a Dozen, based in JP Nagar, Bengaluru, runs a women-led kitchen and supplies corporate clients including Accenture, Yahoo and IndiQube.

Megna Jain's bakery began under a college desk. As an 18-year-old BCom student at Christ University in Bengaluru, she posted her eggless cupcakes on her class WhatsApp group, received an order for 90, and carried baskets of them to college on BMTC buses, decorating them with frosting between classes.

"I would carry baskets and baskets of cupcakes on the BMTC bus. I would decorate them with frosting in college. I hid the cupcakes under my desk and sold them during the break," she told YourStory.

From The Cupcake Booth to Dream a Dozen

Selling mini cupcakes for Rs 20 and larger ones for Rs 40, Jain first named the venture The Cupcake Booth, in vanilla, chocolate and red velvet flavours, and began stocking a college cafeteria and a traditional Kerala cafe. A professor who initially called selling in college "improper" relented after classmates stood up for her; other professors taught her to write a business plan and pitch at competitions.

After college she spent 1.5 years at InnerChef learning how home bakers are onboarded, then trained for three months at Cakewala. In January 2018 she launched Dream a Dozen from her home kitchen, with an initial investment of just Rs 5,000, and within six months had to move to a larger premise. She later recounted the early premises problems plainly: a building caretaker who cut power at peak order times and turned her signboard upside down.

Six weeks shut, then a pivot that doubled sales

In March 2020 Jain moved to a larger space planned as a walk-in bakery. Then COVID-19 arrived. "We were closed for six weeks and I took online classes to sustain the business. We decided to pivot and stick completely to an online model knowing that the pandemic was here to stay for a while," she told YourStory.

The pivot worked through corporate gifting. With Diwali approaching, she approached companies that needed gift boxes sent to staff and customers across India. "We delivered about 1,500 gift boxes, covering our losses and doubling our sales than in any other year in the past," she said. At the time of YourStory's 2021 profile, Dream a Dozen had a 15-member team, an all-women kitchen team of eight, an average order value of around Rs 1,200, and was looking at revenue of Rs 1.2 crore that financial year. Its JP Nagar bakery operated as a centralised kitchen with no walk-in customers.

A women-run kitchen, on principle

In a later interview with SheThePeople, Jain explained why the kitchen stayed women-led. "If you look at the representation of women in [commercial kitchens] you'll always see male chefs," she said, arguing that women employees need to feel safety and belonging at work. She also trains women from less-privileged backgrounds toward financial independence, and has added Indian flavours — besan laddoo cookies, gulab jamun cheesecakes, rabri-jalebi cupcakes — to a menu that began with Western-style cupcakes.

"It is still so astonishing to people and it's really sad. So it's not that I am creating a new path but I wish that [women-led enterprises] are not so rare that it surprises people."

— Megna Jain, founder, Dream a Dozen, to SheThePeople

Jain has said people at early client meetings assumed someone else — a father or a husband — must have funded the business. The record is simpler: Rs 5,000, a WhatsApp group, and cupcakes carried on a city bus.
nri_angle: A Bengaluru founder who turned college cupcake sales into a women-led corporate gifting bakery — a bootstrapped food story diaspora readers follow closely.
